content: The Proterozoic Eon is a significant geological time period that predates the emergence of abundant complex life on Earth. It spans from approximately 2,500 million years ago (Ma) to 542 ± 1 Ma. This eon is the most recent part of the Precambrian time and is divided into three distinct geological eras, listed from oldest to youngest: the Paleoproterozoic, the Mesoproterozoic, and the Neoproterozoic. During the Proterozoic, several critical events occurred. One of the most notable was the transition to an oxygen-rich atmosphere, which took place during the Mesoproterozoic. Additionally, the Proterozoic experienced multiple glaciations, including the hypothesized Snowball Earth event during the Cryogenian period in the late Neoproterozoic. The Ediacaran Period, which lasted from 635 to 542 Ma, marked the evolution of abundant soft-bodied multicellular organisms. The geological record of the Proterozoic is significantly more complete than that of the preceding Archean Eon. Unlike the deep-water deposits characteristic of the Archean, the Proterozoic features extensive shallow epicontinental seas, where many strata were deposited. These rocks are generally less metamorphosed than those from the Archean, with many remaining unaltered. Studies of these rocks reveal that the Proterozoic was marked by rapid and massive continental accretion, unique to this eon, as well as supercontinent cycles and modern-style orogenic (mountain-building) activity. The first known glaciations also occurred during this eon, with one beginning shortly after its onset and at least four others occurring during the Neoproterozoic, culminating in the Snowball Earth event associated with the Varangian glaciation. One of the most transformative events of the Proterozoic was the accumulation of oxygen in Earth's atmosphere. Although photosynthesis had been producing oxygen since the Archean, it could not accumulate significantly until chemical sinks, such as unoxidized sulfur and iron, were saturated. Around 2.3 billion years ago, atmospheric oxygen levels were likely only 1–2% of their current levels. Banded iron formations, which are the primary source of the world's iron ore, acted as a major chemical sink, with most of their accumulation ceasing around 1.9 billion years ago due to increased oxygen levels or more thorough oceanic mixing. The appearance of red beds, which are colored by hematite, indicates a rise in atmospheric oxygen after 2 billion years ago, as these formations are absent in older rocks. The oxygen build-up was likely driven by the saturation of chemical sinks and an increase in carbon burial, which sequestered organic compounds that would otherwise have reacted with atmospheric oxygen. In terms of paleogeography, the Proterozoic was marked by significant geological activity. The Mackenzie dike swarm, located in the Canadian Shield, is the largest known dike swarm on Earth and was a source of massive flood basalt eruptions throughout the Proterozoic. This dike swarm is thought to have originated from a mantle plume center known as the Mackenzie hotspot. Life during the Proterozoic underwent significant advancements. The first complex single-celled and multicellular organisms appeared, coinciding with the accumulation of free oxygen in the atmosphere. This may have been facilitated by an increase in oxidized nitrates, which eukaryotes utilize, unlike cyanobacteria. The Proterozoic also saw the evolution of symbiotic relationships between mitochondria and their eukaryotic hosts, as well as between chloroplasts and their plant or protist hosts. Eukaryotic organisms, such as acritarchs, began to flourish during this time. However, cyanobacteria also thrived, with stromatolites reaching their peak abundance and diversity around 1.2 billion years ago. Traditionally, the boundary between the Proterozoic and the Phanerozoic eons was defined at the base of the Cambrian period, marked by the first appearance of animal fossils such as trilobites and archaeocyathids. Although numerous fossil forms have since been discovered in Proterozoic rocks, the upper boundary of the Proterozoic remains fixed at the base of the Cambrian, currently dated to 542 Ma.
